The beginning of the service is in the heart, and this is the aspect of <term>bittul ha-yesh</term> <gloss>the nullification of the self/the ego</gloss>, and so on. This matter is very deep, and one must understand how <term>bittul ha-yesh</term> is possible within the heart, for the heart is full of desires and wills. How can the self be nullified within the heart? 

The matter is as it is written: "I have hidden Your word in my heart" <note>Psalm 119:11</note>, and the heart is the dwelling place of the soul. The soul consists of the aspects of <term>Chokhmah</term> <gloss>Wisdom</gloss>, <term>Binah</term> <gloss>Understanding</gloss>, and <term>Da'at</term> <gloss>Knowledge</gloss>. When a person contemplates the greatness of God, the "self" that is in the heart is nullified, and this is the aspect of <term>bittul ha-yesh</term>. This is the aspect of the expansion of the soul into the heart. When the soul expands into the heart, the heart is nullified before God, and this is the aspect of <term>bittul ha-yesh</term>. 

This matter is the aspect of the "service of the heart." The service of the heart is the aspect of prayer. In prayer, a person prays to God and asks for mercy, and this is the aspect of the service of the heart. This is the aspect of <term>bittul ha-yesh</term>. When a person prays, he is nullified before God, and this is the aspect of <term>bittul ha-yesh</term>.

Some transfer wonderful signs and <term>altrilogical</term> <gloss>allegorical/other-speaking</gloss> figures from the Cabala, about which it is superfluous to argue further, especially since nothing can be drawn so ineptly that one could not induce some color to it from geometry and lead it to some figure among the elements of languages. For the present, there appears to us no reason why we should defer to the Chemical monad. And so, we do not dislike the industry of those who fashion the characters of essences from whole hieroglyphic notes of infinite kinds, so that it is clearly manifest, provided one is knowledgeable of the original writing, that it is something artificially produced from them, just as the indices of sublimated and precipitated mercury teach. Thus, if one wanted to designate the crocus of Mars and the flower extracted from it, one could form this image: ♁, to indicate the magisterial crocus; as for the flower, this: ♁, or ♁. Dorneiferus poorly observed the foundation when he painted it ♄. If the letter Zeta expressed by the Indian figure of the ternary was meant to designate white lead, the added mark is nevertheless of no art. Because Spanish white is made from white lead through corrosion and reverberatory calcination, it rightfully claims the wood of its matter for itself, and can be painted in its own form ♄. ### CHAP. VII.
### On strengthening, repairing, and obstructing vessels.

<margin>To ch. 3, b. 1 of Alchemy.</margin> We could have added the strengthenings, cements, lids, and the rest to their instruments and vessels. But because artisans, partly by whim, luxuriate in the variety and singularity of special instruments and not rarely show their ingenuity, knowledge, and proprietorship in this way: and partly because the nature of circumstances imposes upon them a certain necessity, so that they are forced to invent something on the spur of the moment in which to perfect the magistery: while some do not even place their work in a multitude of vessels; nay, are accustomed to destroy and dismantle their built furnaces and remove their instruments from sight in moments, so that you can hardly detect the traces of the artisan in the place of elaboration: we have judged it more consultative to throw into one chapter those things which might be found concerning this matter in the commentaries that were at hand, and which we have also approved by our own judgment and experience. From there, let each person take what is convenient for him. Here also, that saying holds: *clearer and more unlearned*. <note>A reference to keeping methods simple.</note> Let him who does not wish to hear about clay depart from this workshop. Certain instruments and vessels must be strengthened with a kind of <term>ichneumonian</term> <gloss>predatory/cunning</gloss> art, or a salamandrine one, against the force of fires and the violence of spirits, and induced and encrusted as if with armor, which also protects against external injuries of collision; indeed, in the weakness of matter in great fires, flight, and melting, hope is often in the crust and external armor, even though metal refiners experience that iron and copper instruments easily escape the force of fires by the protection of clay, as can be seen in the nozzles of bellows and their casings. The Chemist smears with clay, or has vessels—glass, cucurbits, phials, and receptor ampullas—smeared, not only around the bottoms, but also the necks, arms, and nozzles, if a greater force of fire is to be applied, as in the reverberatory furnace, in calcinations, or in gentler distillations, although we are not accustomed to use this material easily even in hot ones, as it is made safe from waters like gypsum. Often a circumspect master uses a bare vessel, which an inexperienced person would not dare to attempt. Truly, it is fitting to know the nature of Vulcan and to do nothing precipitately. We sometimes encrust with clay even dishes and shells to the very bottom, in which we dissolve, coagulate, or dry and color something over the coals. Unless earthen vessels transmit moisture and are made of weak clay, or not sufficiently baked and hardened by the potter's hand, we arm and solidify them with the same care. For this reason, we apply it to both furnaces and crucibles inside and out, as the necessity of the work requires. The same happens also to iron ones that are about to endure a stronger fire. For iron is easily calcined and is even weakened by the strong spirits of fumes. Thus, iron furnaces are encrusted; cement boxes, channels, lids; even the ceilings, beams, and pedestals of that material. Sometimes we smear spoons, casting ladles, and tongs inside and out. ### DE QVANTITATE.

XXXV. Quantum describit Aristoteles hîc lib. 5. tex 18. *Quod est divisibile in ea, quæ insunt, quorum utrumque vel unumquodque unum quid, et hoc aliquid aptum est esse.* Id est (ut quidem P. Suarez interpretatur) quorum v- trumque aptum est naturâ suâ per sese, ut unum quoddam totum, ab alijs separatum, manere, et quidem quantum est ex vi quantitatis, eodem modo di- visibile, divisibilitate scilicet Physicâ, et naturali, vi cuius unum Corpus naturaliter expellit aliud, vel partes eius à loco, quem ante occupabant.

XXXVI. Est sententia, ut ait P. Suarez, inter Thomistas satis vul- garis, primarium quantitatis effectum formalem esse distinctionem par- tium integralium; ita ut sine quantitate nec Materia prima, nec ulla alia entitas materialis aliquas partes integrantes habeat. XXXIII. Regarding Imaginary Time we judge the same as we do regarding Imaginary space, namely that it is in reality nothing, beyond the intrinsic durations of things which found various relations of distance and nearness.

XXXIV. Finally, duration is either created or uncreated. The uncreated is proper to GOD alone, and is called Eternity; and it is defined by <term>Boethius</term> <gloss>Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius, Roman philosopher</gloss>: *The whole, simultaneous, and perfect possession of interminable life.* Created duration is either temporary or perpetual. It is temporary if it has both a beginning and an end. It is perpetual if it at least has no end. Such is the duration of Angels and the rational soul, which is also called <term>Aevum</term> <gloss>the Age or Eon</gloss>, and is commonly defined as: *The uninterrupted permanence of a thing in being once received.*

### ON QUANTITY.

XXXV. <term>Aristotle</term> describes a quantity here in Book 5, text 18: *That which is divisible into those things which are present, of which each one or every one is a certain "one," and this "something" is apt to be.* That is (as Father <term>Suarez</term> indeed interprets) of which each one is apt by its own nature in and of itself, as a certain whole, separated from others, to remain, and indeed, insofar as it is from the force of quantity, divisible in the same way, namely by physical and natural divisibility, by the force of which one Body naturally expels another, or its parts from the place which they previously occupied.

XXXVI. It is an opinion, as Father <term>Suarez</term> says, sufficiently common among the <term>Thomists</term> <gloss>followers of Thomas Aquinas</gloss>, that the primary formal effect of quantity is the distinction of integral parts; so that without quantity neither primary matter nor any other material entity has any integral parts. Father <term>Vasquez</term> <gloss>Gabriel Vázquez, Jesuit theologian</gloss> followed the Thomists among our own in Volume 3, part 3, disputation 190, from number 20. But to the contrary: 1. For just as each thing is a being in and of itself, so it is "one" in and of itself, and consequently divided and distinct from anything else. 2. Because otherwise one would have to proceed to infinity. For if one thing is distinct from another by another third entity, then it must be distinguished from that third by another fourth, and so on to infinity. 3. Because matter is presupposed for quantity with its whole entity. Therefore, it cannot receive parts from it; for since the whole is nothing other than all its parts, that which is presupposed with its whole entity must also be presupposed with its parts. Therefore, the primary formal effect of quantity cannot consist in the distinction of parts.

XLVII. Ego hac in re cum quibusdam R. R. breviter sequentia statuo 1. Partes temporis & durationis continuari immediatè se ipsis. 2. Etiam ubicationes rerum continuarum, ut inter se continuentur, praeter suas entitates, & alias conditiones infrà referendas, nihil intrinsecè requirere, nisi simultaneas durationes. 3. Etiam accidentia symbola, & partes substantiales aliter non continuari nisi per immediatas suarum partium ubicationes simul existentes, modò tres insuper hasce conditiones habeant. 1. Ut sint eiusdem speciei, neque ordinatæ ad constituendum diversa entia per se. Unde non possunt invicem continuari formæ terræ & aquæ, neque diversorum equorum animæ. 2. Ut sint extrema divisibilia in plura rationis eiusdem; ob cuius defectum repugnat continuatio inter duos Angelos, vel duas animas rationales. 3. Ut tales partes non insint diversis entibus per se; & sic repugnat continuari inter se, non solùm elementorum formas, sed etiam materias, quantitates, qualitates, & quæcunque illorum accidentia symbola. Neque enim hæc intelliguntur continua, si ipsorum subiecta tantùm contigua sint.

XLVIII. In continuo vel permanente vel successivo præter partes non datur formaliter ullum indivisibile, neque copulans neque terminans. Ratio est. quia talium indivisibilium non est ulla necessitas. Non ad uniendum? quia partes sufficienter copulantur & uniuntur per ubicationes immediatas, & alias conditiones. Non ad terminandum? Nam sive à Deo realiter, sive à nobis per intellectum auferatur superficies terminativa alicuius tabulæ; illa tabula tam bene erit, & intelligetur finita, atque antè; habebit easdem passiones & usum, quem antè. ## To Bertrandus Eygua, Royal Advocate in the Senate of Toulouse.

Prince, as a patron, O Eygua, patron of the prince,
Tullius <note>Cicero</note> can be mute before you.
While timid eloquence presses the golden fountains,
The impious crowd fears you, the pious crowd reveres you.

## To Cupid.

Clytia recalls the absent one and drives away the one following,
Thus, little Cupid, you drag us here and there.
Tantalus is deluded, thirsty, in the midst of waters.
Thirst always holds me as I am carried in the midst.

## To Franciscus Bertrandus, the fourth President of Toulouse.

Worshipper of sacred laws, most holy president,
Who sing learned poems with a tuneful lyre:
You, I confess, happy, shine with clear honor,
But these things are lesser than your genius.

## Epitaph of the Divine Franciscus, King of the Gauls.

Mars, Phoebus, and Pallas have set up a tomb for the king,
With whom law, poetry, and strong arms lie.

## Epitaph of Nicolaus Bertrandus, the fourth President. To Death.

Death, I see the deed, wretched one, concerning you.
It is not right to deny the penalties for wickedness,
When there is more of reason than in a horse.
You take away, not men, but choice pearls,
Kings, then leaders, and the learned:
And you cast your hands into the holy Senate.
If a limit is not provided for these funerals,
You will be guilty of diminished majesty.
You laugh, I guess what you yourself feel:
You do not fear eternal judgment.

## To Antonius Broullatus Moniayus.

You derive your lineage from an illustrious stem,
Yet you prepare to join sacred laws to your family.
Thus, Broullatus, the glory of a double name adorns you:
What you take from your ancestors, what you beget yourself.

7. Manet itaque Conclusio nostra Vera quod videlicet peculiaris aliqua disciplina Spiritibus in Philosophiâ assignanda sit à reliquis omnibus distincta. Probatum id jam est per remotionem ab illis disciplinis ad quas referri posse videbatur, et porrò probatur argumento gemino: (1) Positâ objecti formalis diversitate diversa ponitur disciplina. Atqui in doctrinâ Spirituum ponitur objecti formalis diversitas. Ergò etiam ponitur diversa disciplina. (2) Si Spiritus in nullâ disciplinâ se habet vel ut principium vel ut affectio, vel ut modus contrahens, ad nullam etiam debet referri. Atqui verum est prius. Ergò et posterius.

6. Nor, indeed, should Pneumatology be referred to Theology. Because (1) these two disciplines rely on diverse principles. For the latter has its principles solely from revelation. But the former has its principles innate from nature, and in part also acquires them through sense, experience, and induction. Because (2) Pneumatology is one of the Theoretical disciplines, whereas Theology itself is practical, or Theoretical-Practical, or mixed. Because (3) Pneumatics neither surpasses all doctrines in dignity nor is it the final doctrine in order; but Theology is the most eminent and final of all if you look at the doctrine, inasmuch as it emanated from God by singular counsel and, by leading us back to God, tends toward where it had come.
